title: Tenali Raman Tale 92

full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya, an enthusiastic patron of the arts, visited the studio of the celebrated royal court painter, Master Raghunath.
The painter unveiled a magnificent landscape depicting a galloping warhorse:
The front half of the horse—its noble head, flaring nostrils, muscular chest, and powerful front legs—was rendered with breathtaking realism, charging forward, while the rear half was hidden behind a picturesque stone wall and flowering oleander bushes.

All the courtiers praised the painting.
However, King Krishnadevaraya, in a critical mood, frowned and pointed at the canvas:
'Raghunath, where is the other half of the horse?
Where are its hind legs? Where is its tail?
Thou hast painted only half a horse! How can I pay full price for half an animal?'

Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, great art does not insult the viewer by spelling out every obvious detail; it speaks to the imagination!
The horse’s rear half is safely behind the wall! A man of refined artistic intellect visualizes the complete steed through the power of his mind!'

The King laughed playfully:
'Tenali, thou art always defending painters.
I give thee one month: paint me a canvas that requires imagination, and if it fails to impress me, thou shalt be fined five hundred gold coins!'

One month later, Tenali Raman arrived at the royal audience hall carrying a large, framed canvas covered with a fine silk cloth.
The King and the courtiers gathered eagerly.
Tenali unveiled the canvas:

The canvas was completely, spotlessly, uniformly white!
Near the bottom edge, there were three tiny strokes of green paint resembling blades of grass, and nothing else!

The King stared, bewildered and annoyed:
'Tenali! What is this? The canvas is empty! What hast thou painted?'

Tenali bowed with supreme dignity:
'Maharaj! This is my masterwork: *The Royal Stallion Grazing on Green Pastures*!'

The King frowned: 'Where is the green pasture?'
Tenali replied: 'The horse ate all the grass, Maharaj! That is why only three tiny blades remain at the bottom!'

The King shouted: 'And where is the horse?'
Tenali smiled with dazzling wit:
'Why, Your Majesty! Having eaten all the grass, do you expect a sensible horse to stand around staring at an empty white canvas?
The horse has already galloped back to the royal stables to drink water!
Apply your royal imagination, Maharaj, and visualize the magnificent steed galloping across the distant hills!'

King Krishnadevaraya was stunned for a moment, then burst into uncontrollable, body-shaking laughter!
'Ha-ha-ha! Tenali, thou hast paid me back for my criticism of Master Raghunath’s painting!'
The King rewarded Tenali with five hundred gold coins, and officially apologized to the court painter, acknowledging that art and imagination must walk hand in hand.
moral: True art invites the imagination to complete the vision; literal-minded criticism reveals only the critic's lack of depth.
